text: Achilles Returns Hector: When the Enemy Becomes Someone's Son Again
Hector has been dead for twelve days.
Achilles still ties his body behind his chariot and drags it around the burial mound of Patroclus.
He did not let his revenge end when he killed Hector.

Patroclus cannot return, so Hector's body continues to bear Achilles' grief. Every morning, the chariot sets off again, as though, as long as the punishment continues, the loss has not quite passed into the past.
The gods protect Hector's body.
It neither decays nor suffers damage from being dragged.
But its preservation has not ended the humiliation.
A dead person can still be treated as a thing through which someone living goes on expressing anger.
The final book of the *Iliad* is often told as a deeply moving scene:
Priam enters the enemy camp to ask Achilles to return his son's body.
One father awakens in another man's son the memory of his own father.
Achilles finally sees the enemy as human again.
This is not wrong.
But if we describe the return of the body entirely as an act in which Priam's fatherly love softens Achilles, we miss something the story has already put in place.
Before Priam arrives, Zeus has made his decision.
Thetis, too, has already conveyed the divine command to her son:
Accept the ransom. Return Hector.
Achilles has agreed.
Meanwhile, Priam is able to pass through the Greek camp because Hermes escorts him inside.
From the outset, then, this return involves more than a sudden flowering of goodwill between two individuals.
Divine command, ransom, escort, and the ordering of war have all helped define what is possible before the meeting takes place.
This does not drain the scene in the tent of meaning.
It simply helps us see more precisely:
Priam did not bring about the return of the body on his own.
What he changed was how Hector and he himself appeared before Achilles.
Priam enters the tent and clasps Achilles' knees.
Then he kisses the hands that have killed so many of his sons.
This is no uncomplicated gesture of reconciliation.
He has not forgotten what those hands have done.
Nor does he demand that Achilles first prove he is no longer an enemy before making his request.
He simply places himself in the most vulnerable position and says:
Think of your father.
Peleus is old, as I am.
At least he can still hope each day that you will return alive.
I have come here to recover the son you killed.
Priam does not say that Hector never killed Patroclus.
Nor does he say that there is no war between Troy and the Greeks.
He does not build his plea by denying Achilles' reasons.
He does something else:
He reconnects the Hector whom Achilles already knows with a relationship Achilles has not yet faced.
Hector is not only the man who killed Patroclus.
He is also the son whom Priam has risked crossing the enemy camp to bring home.
These two identities do not cancel each other out.
If being a son meant that Hector was no longer an enemy on the battlefield, the story would lose the weight of war.
If being an enemy meant that, in death, Hector was nothing but an object of revenge, the story would compress an entire person into his battlefield role.
“Enemy” is a real identity.
It can explain why Achilles and Hector fought, and why the death of Patroclus brought revenge to this point.
But it cannot fully determine:
How the dead man's body may be treated.
Whether his family still has a claim to bury him.
Whether a city still has a claim to time in which to mourn him.
An identity may give reasons for certain actions without thereby acquiring ownership over every relationship a person has.
Priam's words make Achilles think of his father.
He begins to weep.
But he and Priam are not weeping for the same person.
Priam lies on the ground, mourning Hector.
Achilles weeps first for Peleus, then for Patroclus.
The tent does not fill with a grief that is finally the same for both men.
It is two griefs, neither a substitute for the other, that can exist together for a time.
This matters greatly.
Many stories of reconciliation portray a true encounter as the moment when:
Both sides finally discover that they are really alike.
But Priam and Achilles are not alike.
One has lost his son.
The other has lost his closest companion in arms and has killed the first man's son with his own hands.
They occupy different positions and still belong to opposing sides.
Weeping together does not erase these differences.
It simply means that neither man's grief can any longer occupy the entire room.
Achilles then helps the old man to his feet.
He is willing to return the body.
But this does not make him entirely calm.
When Priam presses to see Hector at once, Achilles still warns him not to provoke his anger further.
He even says that, if the old man continues to trouble his heart, he may defy the gods' command and turn on the man who has come to supplicate him.
This is not someone whose moral transformation is complete.
His anger remains.
Violence may still return.
And that is precisely what makes his next arrangements so convincing.
He orders Hector's body to be washed, anointed, and dressed out of Priam's sight.
Not because the body does not belong to the father.
But because he knows that, if Priam sees his son's body now, the father's anger may rekindle his own.
He does not pretend that they are already safe with each other.
He uses distance to keep the violence still within him from immediately taking over his actions.
Sometimes a boundary does not arise because all inner conflict has gone.
Quite the opposite.
It comes from knowing that the conflict remains, and therefore not allowing the most dangerous next step to happen too easily.
Achilles himself lifts the body onto a bier.
Then he speaks once more to Patroclus.
He asks his dead friend not to be angry with him for returning Hector, and promises to offer him the share of the ransom that should be his.
This brief passage complicates the return.
In answering Priam, Achilles does not declare that he has put Patroclus behind him.
He still needs to explain himself to his dead friend.
Within his world of relationships, returning Hector may still look like a betrayal of Patroclus.
Responding to a new plea, then, does not require him first to declare an old loyalty mistaken.
What actually happens is that he begins to set limits on how much that old loyalty may demand of him.
Avenging Patroclus has already led him to kill Hector.
But it no longer follows that continuing to possess and humiliate the body is justified.
The grief remains valid.
Not every means it employs remains valid.
Priam pays a ransom.
This, too, must not be left out.
Hector's body is not returned unconditionally between two people of equal standing.
An old king brings treasures into the tent of his son's killer to buy his son back.
That gives the encounter a disparity of power that cannot be romanticized away.
Achilles controls the body and whether the old man can leave safely.
Priam must plead, pay, and rely on divine protection.
To speak only of the feelings these fathers and sons share would erase this inequality from the story.
Yet the ransom does not wholly subsume the personal encounter either.
Once Achilles accepts the goods, he does more than complete an exchange.
He eats with Priam, arranges a place for him to rest, and asks how much time Troy needs to hold the funeral.
Priam says:
Nine days of mourning, cremation on the tenth, a burial mound on the eleventh, and on the twelfth, if they must, a return to battle.
Achilles agrees to hold the army back during this time.
What he grants is not peace.
It is time enough for a funeral to take place.
This may be the most important limit in the entire scene.
Returning the body does not end the war.
Achilles does not join Troy.
Nor does Priam reach an agreement with the Greeks about the causes of the war.
After the funeral, fighting may resume.
This book thus leaves us with an answer more difficult, and more usable, than “compassion ends conflict”:
Some boundaries need not wait for a conflict to be resolved before they hold.
Both sides may still believe they have reasons to fight.
May still mourn different dead.
May still be unable to forgive all that has happened.
And yet they can still acknowledge:
The body should be returned.
The funeral should take place.
Mourning takes time.
Being an enemy is not enough to cancel these claims.
The most basic restraints are not a reward granted after reconciliation.
They are precisely what keeps conflict from swallowing everything while reconciliation has yet to come.
Of course, this cannot be turned into a simple formula for every situation of war.
The return of Hector is supported by divine will, ransom, a personal plea, and the shared customs of the epic world.
Opposing sides in reality may not share such traditions, nor have an Achilles who can restrain an army on his own.
A personal encounter can change a decision, but it cannot do all the work at the level of institutions and the structures of war.
If every basic limit must wait for a victor suddenly to remember his father, the limits themselves are too fragile.
Truly stable restraints cannot depend solely on the most fortunate moments of feeling.
Yet a personal encounter can still do something that institutional language sometimes cannot:
Allow a person wholly obscured by a role to appear again through particular relationships.
Not to prove that rules are no longer needed.
But to help the rules remember whom they were meant to protect.
When Hector returns to Troy, Cassandra is the first to see his body on the wagon.
Andromache, Hecuba, and Helen each lament him.
The Hector each has lost is different:
A husband.
A son.
One of the few people in the city who still treated Helen with kindness.
When Priam says “my son” in the tent, he has not said all there is to say about Hector.
He has merely opened the first breach, so that Achilles can no longer lock the body entirely within the single name “my enemy.”
A person never exists only within the relationship in which they come into conflict with me.
Even when that relationship is very real, and has already caused irreparable harm.
Achilles returns Hector not because Hector has suddenly become innocent.
Nor because revenge has become wholly without reason.
He returns a body he can control, but whose entire meaning he cannot therefore claim as his own.
Priam lets him see:
The man dragged behind the chariot also belongs to other people's memories, responsibilities, mourning, and futures.
The enemy becomes someone's son again.
But he does not thereby cease to be an enemy.
It is precisely because both things are true that the return has real weight.
It is not reconciliation.
It is a refusal to let war possess everything, even when reconciliation has not yet arrived, and may never arrive at all.

*Textual basis: Book 24 of Homer's Iliad, especially the gods' decision to return the body, Thetis conveying the divine command to Achilles, Priam's entry into the camp and his plea, the two men's separate mourning, the washing and return of the body, and the arrangements for resuming battle after the twelfth day (approximately 24.1–21, 110–140, 468–676, 695–804). This essay does not present Priam's personal plea as the sole cause of the body's return, nor interpret the limited funeral truce as reconciliation in the war.*
